explanations.explanation: That's the exact phrase. Job says, "I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all." (Job 16:2) Eliphaz, one of his three friends (Job 2:11), had just finished his speech (Job 15). I bet Job was hoping for a hug and got a lecture instead.

Nope, Job isn't handing out compliments here. He says, "miserable comforters are you all." (Job 16:2) His three friends came to sympathize with him and comfort him (Job 2:11), and Job calls them miserable comforters. Think of a friend who brings you a cookie box with nothing in it.

Job doesn't call them wise at all. He says, "miserable comforters are you all." (Job 16:2) Later he even tells them he won't find a wise man among them (Job 17:10). So "wise old teachers" is not how Job sees this crowd.

Yes, he says it. Job tells his friends, "I could also speak like you if you were in my place; I could heap up words against you and shake my head at you." (Job 16:4) He knows how to talk like that. The next verse says what he'd do instead.

This one is true, friend. Job says, "I could also speak like you if you were in my place; I could heap up words against you and shake my head at you." (Job 16:4) He's saying he could give the same kind of speech. In the very next verse he says what he would do instead.

That's it. Job says, "But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief." (Job 16:5) He knows what real comfort sounds like, and it doesn't sound like a lecture. Honestly, that's a good rule for anybody visiting a hurting friend.

Close to what his friends were doing, but not what Job says he'd do. He says, "But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief." (Job 16:5) The word is encourage, and relief is what he'd be going for. Correcting is the speech he's tired of hearing.

Job doesn't say he'd grill them. He says, "But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief." (Job 16:5) Encouragement and relief are the goal. Nobody ever felt better after a coworker fired off a list of questions on a hard day.
Right. Job says, "Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family." (Job 16:7) That's the weight he's carrying. I think this one hurts.
Fields aren't what Job names here. He says, "You have devastated all my family." (Job 16:7) His loss runs deeper than land or crops. I think this part is the heaviest thing he says in the verse.
Job doesn't mention cities at all. He says, "You have devastated all my family." (Job 16:7) It's personal. He's talking about the people closest to him.

Yes, that's what Job says. "God has delivered me to unjust men; He has thrown me to the clutches of the wicked." (Job 16:11) These are Job's own words about how it feels to him. A heavy verse, so we just let it sit and read it plainly.

This one is true, friend. Job says, "God has delivered me to unjust men; He has thrown me to the clutches of the wicked." (Job 16:11) It's a hard thing to say out loud. Job says it anyway, and the text lets him.
Target is the word. Job says, "He has set me up as His target…" (Job 16:12) Right after, he talks about archers surrounding him (Job 16:13). That's how it feels to Job, and he says it plainly.
Footstool isn't the word Job uses in this verse. He says, "He has set me up as His target…" (Job 16:12) The next verse brings in archers (Job 16:13), so target fits the picture. It's target, friend.
Servant isn't the word Job uses in this verse. He says, "He has set me up as His target…" (Job 16:12) Archers come next, and archers need something to aim at. So it's target, friend.
Yes, violence goes in the first blank. Job says, "…yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) He's standing by his innocence even while he's hurting. That takes backbone.

Yes, pure goes in the second blank. Job says, "…yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) Even with all that sorrow, he says his prayer is pure. He keeps praying, and I respect that.

Anger doesn't fit this verse. Job says, "…yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) Violence is what his hands are free of. Anger would be a different claim, and Job doesn't make it here.
Silent isn't Job's word. He says, "…yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) The blank wants pure, friend.

Job does talk about being frail earlier (Job 16:8), but weak isn't what he says about his prayer. He says, "…my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) Pure is the word that fills that blank.
Careful, this one flips it. Job says the opposite: "O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest." (Job 16:18) He doesn't want his cry buried. He wants it heard.

Right, it's false. Job says, "O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest." (Job 16:18) He asks for the opposite: no covering of his blood, and no resting for his cry for help.
In heaven is right. Job says, "Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." (Job 16:19) In the middle of all that pain, he looks up. I think that's a bright spot in a dark chapter.
The city gate isn't where Job points. He says, "Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." (Job 16:19) His witness is in heaven, friend.

His friends are the last place Job looks for a witness. Just a verse later he says, "My friends are my scoffers…" (Job 16:20) He says, "Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." (Job 16:19) So it's heaven, friend.

That's right. Job says, "Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!" (Job 16:21) He wishes a man could plead with God the way he would plead with his neighbor. It's a wish, and he says it out loud.

This one is true, friend. Job says, "Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!" (Job 16:21) Look at the comparison: pleading with God, the way a man pleads with his neighbor. That's the wish, right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: He will go the way of no return
explanations.explanation: That's the line. Job says, "For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return." (Job 16:22) He's looking at the end of his life, and he doesn't sugarcoat it. This part is heavy, so we just let it be heavy.

explanations.answer: He will move to a far country
explanations.explanation: Not a move, friend. Job says, "For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return." (Job 16:22) He's talking about the end of his life. This part is heavy, so we let it be heavy.

explanations.answer: He will stand before the king
explanations.explanation: No king in this verse. Job says, "For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return." (Job 16:22) He's looking toward the end of his days. A king's court is somewhere you can walk back out of.

Mockers is right. Job says, "Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion." (Job 17:2) He's got the grave ahead and mockers all around. That's a rough view from where he's sitting.

Mourners isn't the word. Job says, "Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion." (Job 17:2) Mockers are what he sees. I think he'd want comfort, and that makes this view even harder.

Elders aren't mentioned in this verse. Job says, "Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion." (Job 17:2) It's mockers, friend. Not the kind of crowd you want around when you're hurting.
Other way around, friend. Job says, "You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them." (Job 17:4) Exalted is exactly what he says they will not be.
Right, it's false. Job says, "You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them." (Job 17:4) Exalted is exactly what Job says they won't be. Good catch.
Face is the word. Job says, "He has made me a byword among the people, a man in whose face they spit." (Job 17:6) That's about as disrespectful as it gets. Job doesn't hide how bad it feels.
Path isn't the word here. Job says, "…a man in whose face they spit." (Job 17:6) Spitting in someone's face is personal and direct. It's face, friend.
Tent doesn't fit this verse. Job says, "…a man in whose face they spit." (Job 17:6) The spitting is in his face. Face is the word that fills the blank.

Yes. Job says, "The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless." (Job 17:8) The upright look at what's happening and they're shocked. Job says it plainly, so we take it plainly.
Not pleased at all. Job says, "The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless." (Job 17:8) Appalled is the word. Nobody upright is throwing a party here.
Looking away isn't what Job says. He says, "The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless." (Job 17:8) Appalled is the word he uses for the upright.

Stronger is right. Job says, "Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger." (Job 17:9) Even in the middle of all this pain, Job says that. That's a man holding on, friend.

You might expect weaker after all of Job's sorrow, but that's not what he says. He says, "…the one with clean hands grows stronger." (Job 17:9) The word is stronger. Job says it right in the middle of his hardest chapter.
Quieter isn't in this verse. Job says, "…the one with clean hands grows stronger." (Job 17:9) Job himself is anything but quiet in this passage. Stronger is the word that fits.
Job says the opposite. He tells them, "For I will not find a wise man among you." (Job 17:10) A wise man is exactly what he says he won't find.

Right, false. Job tells his friends, "But come back and try again, all of you. For I will not find a wise man among you." (Job 17:10) He doesn't expect to find a wise man in the bunch. That's him being honest.

That's the question. Job asks, "…where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?" (Job 17:15) He's picturing Sheol as his home, and the question just hangs there. It's a heavy moment, and the text lets it stay heavy.
Burial isn't what Job asks about. He asks, "…where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?" (Job 17:15) The question is about hope. It's the one that follows him out of the chapter.
Job doesn't ask where his friends are. He asks, "…where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?" (Job 17:15) His question is about hope.
Yes, that's how he ends it. Job asks, "Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?" (Job 17:16) It's a question, not an answer. And the story keeps going after it.
This one is true, friend. Job ends with, "Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?" (Job 17:16) He closes on a question. The story isn't over, though.
